title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
The page closes Corollary 1 (§44), which noted that the higher simple tones bring in one, two or three nodes in turn. It then gives Corollary 2 (§45) and opens the Scholion (§46).

Setting. On the previous pages Euler solved the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation y_tt + K y_xxxx = 0 by separating variables for the various end conditions. Each mode has the time factor sin(ζ + t·ω²·c·√(2gb)/a²). Here a is the length, c the 'thickness', b the absolute elasticity of the material (with gravity g used to convert units), and ω a root of the frequency equation for the given end conditions (for example cos ω·cosh ω = ±1). So the angular frequency is ω_n² c√(2gb)/a².

§45 (Corollary 2). These formulas compare all tones of one rod under different end conditions, since only ω_n changes. They also compare different rods, provided the cross-sections are geometrically similar (for example all circular). Then the frequency is proportional to c/a²: directly as the diameter and inversely as the square of the length. A thicker rod of the same length sounds higher, and a longer rod of the same thickness sounds lower 'in duplicate ratio'.

In modern terms f_n = (β_n L)²/(2π L²)·√(EI/(ρA)). The radius of gyration √(I/A) scales linearly with the cross-section size, which gives f ∝ d/L².

§46 (Scholion, begins). Euler extends the result to non-circular sections, starting with a rectangle ABCD (Tab. III, Fig. 5). There are two principal bending directions. The next page completes the point: the relevant c is the side lying in the plane of bending, and the other side drops out entirely, because I/A depends only on h for a rectangle.
errors: No errors on this page; the scaling f ∝ c/a² for similar cross-sections is correct.

Next page, not this one: Euler states that for a circular section c = (3/4)·AB. Matching I/A between a rectangle (h²/12) and a circle (d²/16) instead gives h = (√3/2)d ≈ 0.866d, so c² = (3/4)AB². This looks like a slip, or a different convention, in which c was written for c².

ideas.what: Frequency of transverse rod vibration scales as thickness/length² for geometrically similar sections
ideas.modern_name: Scaling law of Euler–Bernoulli beam natural frequencies, f ∝ √(EI/ρA)/L² ∝ h/L²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1742–1744); confirmed experimentally by Chladni (1787)
ideas.where_published: Euler, E65 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I De curvis elasticis (1744); E526; discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11.2)

ideas.what: Comparison of all tones of one rod under different end conditions via the roots ω of the frequency equation
ideas.modern_name: Mode-dependent eigenvalue factor (β_n L)² for different boundary conditions
ideas.where_published: E526 and earlier Euler and D. Bernoulli memoirs on elastic rods

ideas.what: For a rectangular section, only the dimension in the bending plane matters; the width drops out
ideas.modern_name: Bending about the principal axes; I/A = h²/12 is independent of width
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Euler's moment of stiffness; standard in later beam theory (Navier and others)

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds a well-known scaling corollary and the start of a routine scholion on cross-section shape. All of it is documented in Truesdell's history of the subject.
transcription_corrections: The horizontal line through 'cari possunt, dummodo crassities in omnibus fuerit similis' is a scan artifact, not a deletion; the transcription correctly keeps the text.
